correctness.rationale: On the complete graph's edge set, total domination means at most one isolated ground vertex and no component K2: an unselected pair only needs a selected edge at either endpoint, while a selected pair needs a different incident edge. For t covered vertices, c nontrivial components and m selected edges, c <= floor(t/3) and m >= t-c. At the claimed optimum with n=3k, zero isolates forces k trees of size three; one isolate forces k-1 trees with surplus two vertices above size three. The surplus is either two in one component or one in each of two. For residues 1 and 2, no-isolate graphs exceed the bound, and with one isolate the forced surplus is zero and one, respectively. These forests attain the bound, including n=4,5,6 and the first two-four-vertex case n=9. Dividing by component-order factorials and permutations of equal-size components and multiplying by the Prüfer counts 3, 16 and 125 gives the displayed coefficients, and the isolation proportion is the ratio of the all-P3 profile to the total. A fresh exhaustive open-neighborhood union replay at the proved minimum reproduced all seven totals and all profiles for n=4..10, checking foresthood for each accepted set; it is supplemental to the general argument.
residual_risks: No formal proof or external attestation; the replay at fixed minimum does not establish the minimum or the all-n classification independently of the proof.

value.rationale: Classifying all optimum configurations of a natural graph family is a worthwhile goal, and the proof is readable. As a distinct scientific contribution, however, the frozen claim recomputes the already indexed exact classification and labelled counts. The isolation statement is a direct consequence of those counts and no independent new structural or enumerative remainder is supplied.
residual_risks: This does not dispute pedagogical or reproducibility value, or assert historical priority beyond the established overlap.
